Overview

Higher-order expressivity, without higher-order message passing

Higher-order message passing (HOMP) models multi-way interactions but scales poorly. HOPSE computes positional and structural encodings once, on Hasse graphs, then trains only MLPs.

Abstract

While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective at modeling relational data, pairwise connections cannot fully capture multi-way relationships naturally present in complex real-world systems. In response to this, Topological Deep Learning (TDL) leverages more general combinatorial representations —such as simplicial or cellular complexes— to accommodate higher-order interactions. Existing TDL methods often extend GNNs through Higher-Order Message Passing (HOMP), but face critical scalability challenges due to the steep complexity overhead of propagating messages through combinatorial structures.

To overcome this limitation, we propose HOPSE (Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder), a framework free of learnable message passing layers that uses Hasse graph decompositions to derive efficient and expressive encodings over arbitrary higher-order domains. Notably, HOPSE training and inference scale linearly with the size of combinatorial representations while preserving the expressive power and permutation equivariance of the HOMP approaches. Experiments on molecular and topological benchmarks show that it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance while consistently achieving speedups over HOMP-based models, opening a new path for scalable TDL. The code is available at github.com/geometric-intelligence/topobench.git.

At a glance

  • 7/12benchmarks where the best HOPSE variant has the best mean score
  • 2.5×faster training than HOMP models (geometric mean, excluding one-time preprocessing), up to 20×
  • 0learnable message-passing layers: encodings are computed once, then only MLPs train
  • 8+4molecular benchmarks plus MANTRA topological benchmarks

Background

Complexes, neighborhoods and Hasse graphs

Combinatorial complexes hold cells of several ranks (nodes, edges, faces). Each neighborhood function turns a complex into an ordinary directed graph, its strictly augmented Hasse graph, on which any graph encoding can run.

Combinatorial complex

A triple T=(V,C,rk)\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{C},\mathrm{rk})T=(V,C,rk): nodes V\mathcal{V}V, cells C⊆P(V)∖∅\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{V})\setminus\emptysetC⊆P(V)∖∅, and an order-preserving rank function. A cell of rank kkk is a kkk-cell; it subsumes graphs, simplicial and cell complexes.

Neighborhoods

A neighborhood function N:C→P(C)\mathcal{N}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{C})N:C→P(C) maps each cell to its neighbors: adjacencies At,s\mathcal{A}_{t,s}At,s​ link cells of the same rank ttt through cells of rank sss; incidences Is→t\mathcal{I}_{s\to t}Is→t​ link rank sss to rank ttt.

Strictly augmented Hasse graph

GN=(CN,EN)G_{\mathcal{N}}=(\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{N}},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{N}})GN​=(CN​,EN​) with CN={σ∣N(σ)≠∅}\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{N}}=\{\sigma\mid\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\neq\emptyset\}CN​={σ∣N(σ)=∅} and EN={(τ,σ)∣τ∈N(σ)}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{N}}=\{(\tau,\sigma)\mid\tau\in\mathcal{N}(\sigma)\}EN​={(τ,σ)∣τ∈N(σ)}. Strictly: only cells with at least one neighbor are kept.

Why higher-order message passing scales poorly

A rank-RRR complex admits 2(R+1)R2(R+1)R2(R+1)R neighborhood functions, and HOMP models must choose how to compose them into message passing routes. Restricting to minimal routes, which update every rank exactly once, already leaves (R+1)!(R+1)!(R+1)! options; on top of this search space, propagating messages is computationally demanding. HOPSE avoids composing routes: it selects an unordered set of neighborhoods, encodes each Hasse graph once before training, and needs no message passing during training.

Method

Encode Hasse graphs once, then train only MLPs

Every structure-dependent computation happens before training. Steps A–C run once per dataset with no gradients; steps D and E are MLPs applied to each cell independently, and step F is the task readout.

Two realizations

Handcrafted or pretrained encoders

The choice of encoders G defines the two realizations, trading preprocessing cost against representational richness. Both aggregate with concatenation and use MLPs for every learnable map.

HOPSE-M

Handcrafted graph encodings: LapPE, ElectrostaticPE, RWSE, HKdiagSE (connectivity-only) or HKFE, KHopFE, PPRFE (feature-aware).

HOPSE-GPSE

A pretrained GPSE encoder supplies the encodings, avoiding eigendecompositions.

  • A single encoder, G={g1}\mathbf{G}=\{g_1\}G={g1​} with g1=GPSE(⋅)g_1=\mathrm{GPSE}(\cdot)g1​=GPSE(⋅), a GNN pretrained to produce positional and structural representations with standard message passing.
  • Following GPSE’s pre-training protocol, Hasse-graph cells are fed random noise, Fr,k∼N(0,I)∈R20F_{r,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\in\mathbb{R}^{20}Fr,k​∼N(0,I)∈R20; the cells’ original attributes are preserved and injected downstream (step D).
  • Encoders pretrained on ZINC and MolPCBA are evaluated; the corpus is treated as a categorical hyperparameter (ablation).
  • Suited to large complexes with many cells, offering a scalable alternative without significant loss in expressiveness. GPSE has its own limits in expressivity and generalization; it showcases pretrained models as encoders.

Neighborhood sets

Which Hasse graphs to encode is a design choice. The paper evaluates adjacency-based and incidence-based sets of increasing size; the largest ones aggregate up and down relations, including second-order rank jumps.

Spectral encodings require symmetric operators, so Hasse graphs are made undirected before encoding: reciprocal incidences such as I0→1\mathcal{I}_{0\to1}I0→1​ and I1→0\mathcal{I}_{1\to0}I1→0​ collapse to the same graph.

Theory

Strictly more expressive than CCWL, and permutation equivariant

Without any learnable message passing, HOPSE keeps the guarantees of higher-order message passing: under the conditions of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 it distinguishes non-isomorphic complexes at least as well as the CCWL test, sometimes strictly better, and is equivariant to cell permutations.

Theorem 4.1 Expressivity

HOPSE is more powerful than the CCWL test in distinguishing non-isomorphic combinatorial complexes if the functions εr(⋅)\varepsilon_r(\cdot)εr​(⋅), ψk(⋅)\psi_k(\cdot)ψk​(⋅), fr,k(⋅)f_{r,k}(\cdot)fr,k​(⋅), and Θr(⋅)\Theta_r(\cdot)Θr​(⋅) are injective for all k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}k∈{1,…,K} and for all r∈{0,…,R}r\in\{0,\dots,R\}r∈{0,…,R} and gk(⋅)g_k(\cdot)gk​(⋅) is equally expressive as the WL test on the corresponding Hasse graph for at least one k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}k∈{1,…,K}.

If some gk is as discriminative as WL on its Hasse graph, the injective maps carry every difference it detects through to the cell representations, so HOPSE is at least as powerful as CCWL. Strictness follows from a pair of complexes that CCWL cannot separate but HOPSE can (below).

Theorem 4.2 Equivariance

HOPSE is cell permutation equivariant if the functions εr(⋅)\varepsilon_r(\cdot)εr​(⋅), gk(⋅)g_k(\cdot)gk​(⋅), ψk(⋅)\psi_k(\cdot)ψk​(⋅), fr,k(⋅)f_{r,k}(\cdot)fr,k​(⋅), and Θr(⋅)\Theta_r(\cdot)Θr​(⋅) are cell permutation equivariant for all k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}k∈{1,…,K} and all r∈{0,…,R}r\in\{0,\dots,R\}r∈{0,…,R}.

Compositions of equivariant functions are equivariant. In practice this holds because the MLPs are applied row-wise, with shared weights, across the rank-r cells.

O(∑r=0R∣EGNr∣⋅Dr)\mathcal{O}\Big(\textstyle\sum_{r=0}^{R} |E_{G_{\mathcal{N}_r}}|\cdot D_r\Big)O(∑r=0R​∣EGNr​​​∣⋅Dr​)

CHOPSEgraph=O(L∣V∣D2K)C_{\mathrm{HOPSE}}^{\text{graph}} = \mathcal{O}\big(L|V|D^2K\big)CHOPSEgraph​=O(L∣V∣D2K)

HOPSE activation memory scales with the number of cells only:

O(∑r=0RNr⋅Dr)\mathcal{O}\Big(\textstyle\sum_{r=0}^{R} N_r\cdot D_r\Big)O(∑r=0R​Nr​⋅Dr​)

On a graph HOPSE is cheaper whenever ∣E∣+∣V∣D>∣V∣DK⋅L/LGNN|E| + |V|D > |V|DK\cdot L/L_{\mathrm{GNN}}∣E∣+∣V∣D>∣V∣DK⋅L/LGNN​; with small KKK (e.g. K=4K=4K=4 for HOPSE-M-C) it is significantly faster on dense graphs with ∣E∣≫∣V∣|E|\gg|V|∣E∣≫∣V∣. Its MLP depth is also independent of the graph diameter, whereas GNNs need depth that grows with the range of interactions. In practice, top configurations pick multi-scale encodings, so peak VRAM can still be higher than some baselines (see parameters).

Results

Competitive accuracy at a fraction of the training time

HOPSE is benchmarked under TopoBench’s standardized protocol against GNNs and state-of-the-art HOMP networks on eight molecular datasets, lifted to simplicial and cell complexes, and on four MANTRA benchmarks of purely topological tasks: homeomorphism type (NAME), orientability (ORIENT) and Betti numbers (β₁, β₂).

Accuracy

Best mean score on 7 of 12 benchmarks

Comparing the best HOPSE variant with the best baseline on each benchmark, HOPSE has the higher mean on MUTAG, NCI1, NCI109, BBB, Cl.Hep., β₁ and β₂. In the paper’s own markup, a HOPSE model is the top performer on MUTAG (HOPSE-M-C (cell)), NCI1 (HOPSE-GPSE (cell)), NCI109 (HOPSE-GPSE (cell)), BBB (HOPSE-GPSE (cell)), Cl.Hep. (HOPSE-GPSE (cell)), β₁ (HOPSE-M-C (simplicial)) and β₂ (HOPSE-M-C (simplicial)).

On the pure topological tasks HOPSE-M-C, a message-passing-free model, sets the best β₁ and β₂, is statistically tied with SCCNN on ORIENT and is a close second on NAME. GNN baselines were evaluated with and without the same encodings HOPSE uses, and Table 1 reports their best configuration (see ablation).

Training time vs HOMP

2.5× faster on average, up to 20×

HOPSE pays a one-time preprocessing cost (see preprocessing), then trains MLPs only. Each mark below is a HOMP model’s training time divided by that of the fastest HOPSE variant in the same domain; the geometric mean over all 40 comparisons is 2.55× end-to-end (2.25× per epoch), and the largest gap is SCCNN on ORIENT at 20.3×.

Measured against every model in the domain, a HOPSE variant is the fastest or not significantly slower in 16 of 20 dataset–domain columns of end-to-end time (fastest outright in 13), and in 20 of 20 for time per epoch. The end-to-end exceptions are PROTEINS (simplicial, fastest: TopoTune); Cl.Hep. (simplicial, fastest: TopoTune); BBB (cell, fastest: TopoTune); Cl.Hep. (cell, fastest: TopoTune).

Efficiency

A one-time preprocessing cost, and a parameter trade-off

HOPSE moves every structure-dependent computation into preprocessing and replaces message passing with MLPs over richer inputs. Both choices have a price, reported here in full.

Preprocessing

Encoding cost grows with the neighborhood set

Encodings are extracted once per dataset, before training. Moving from Adj-1 to Adj-3 or Inc-2 generally raises the overhead; in the paper’s markup Adj-1 is the fastest configuration in 20 of 20 dataset–domain columns. On the large MANTRA complexes, preprocessing takes between 203 s and 1690 s depending on variant and neighborhood set: a one-time overhead that the paper finds is heavily offset during training, increasingly so on larger datasets.

Total preprocessing time in seconds per neighborhood set (linear scale within each panel). The accent bar is the fastest set for the selected variant; a ring marks the configuration the paper bolds as fastest across all variants in the domain. MANTRA panels appear for the simplicial domain only.

Parameters

More parameters, less computation

Replacing neighborhood aggregation with rich encodings means HOPSE relies on more expressive, parameter-dense MLPs. In the simplicial domain HOPSE-M-C uses a median of 904k parameters against 774k for SCCNN. In the cell domain the gap is wider: HOPSE medians range from 565k to 910k against 349k for CWN, although all three variants use fewer parameters than CWN on NCI1 (HOPSE-M-C 916k, HOPSE-M-F 571k, HOPSE-GPSE 740k; CWN 1.15M), and HOPSE-M-C also does on Cl.Hep. Every model is evaluated at its own performance-optimized capacity, and GNN baselines tend to select smaller configurations.

Ablations

What matters, and where

Five studies isolate the design choices: which Hasse graphs to encode, which encodings, which GPSE pre-training corpus, and whether the same encodings would suffice to lift GNN or HOMP baselines.

Every plot shows the paper’s significance markup:
best (bold in the paper) not significantly different from best other ± std

Neighborhood sets · Table 7

Topological tasks need the full adjacency set

On NAME, ORIENT and the Betti numbers the richest adjacency set matters most: with Adj-3, which aggregates up and down relations across dimensions including second-order rank jumps, HOPSE-M-C holds the best mean on all four MANTRA benchmarks (93.96 on NAME, 83.94 on ORIENT), while its incidence-only sets fall far behind (Inc-2: 76.04 and 58.34). For molecular tasks, simpler sets such as Adj-1 and Adj-2 often perform competitively, acting as a regularizer while staying cheap; HOPSE-M-C reaches 88.09 on MUTAG (cell) with Adj-1 alone.

Test mean ± std per neighborhood set, one panel per benchmark on its own scale; significance is computed within each model–domain block. TopoTune is included as a HOMP reference.

Single encodings · Table 8

LapPE unlocks the topological tasks; no encoding wins everywhere

Evaluated one at a time, encodings show dataset-dependent behaviour. On the pure topological tasks spectral information is decisive: with Adj-3, LapPE has the best mean on all four MANTRA benchmarks, reaching 92.39 on NAME, about 16 points above the feature-based encodings. On molecular data RWSE and ElectrostaticPE are strong; ElectrostaticPE is best on MUTAG and CYP3A4 with Adj-1, and PPRFE peaks on BBB with Adj-3. Single encodings occasionally beat combined ones, so encoding sets should be calibrated to the task.

View
Neighborhoods

Each panel compares the seven encodings used alone with the selected neighborhood set; significance is computed within each neighborhood block.

GPSE pre-training corpus · Table 9

No universal pre-training corpus

GPSE encoders pre-trained on MolPCBA and on ZINC both provide useful encodings, but neither dominates: MolPCBA has the higher mean on 7 benchmarks, ZINC on 3, with 2 exact ties, and only on Cl.Hep. is the difference statistically significant. This task dependence is why the corpus is treated as a categorical hyperparameter.

View

PSEs in GNN baselines · Table 10

Encodings help GNNs, case by case

For a fair comparison, GCN, GAT and GIN are run without encodings (×), with feature encodings (F) and with connectivity encodings (C), and Table 1 reports their best configuration. Encodings boost the baselines on several datasets such as MUTAG and NCI1, but there is no single dominant type: C gives the largest MUTAG gains for GAT and GIN, while F works best for GCN on the same dataset.

PSEs in HOMP baselines · Table 11

Adding the encodings to HOMP helps in 13 of 40 cases

Each HOMP baseline was re-run with its best-validation hyperparameters and rank-0 features augmented with CombinedPE. Gains are dataset-dependent rather than systematic: the mean improves for all five models on Caco2 and four of five on MUTAG, but rarely elsewhere, and no augmented baseline overtakes the best method of any column in Table 1, indicating that HOPSE’s advantage stems from its architecture, not merely from the encodings.

Setup

Experimental protocol and reproducibility

All models run under TopoBench’s standardized protocol, with common encoders and readouts. HOPSE is integrated into the open-source TopoBench, including the hyperparameter search configurations and ablation scripts.

Datasets

TUDataset
MUTAG, PROTEINS, NCI1, NCI109Inductive graph classification, kept for comparability with prior work.
Therapeutics Data Commons
BBB, CYP3A4, Cl.Hep., Caco2Clinically relevant molecular property prediction (BBB_Martins, CYP3A4_Veith, Clearance_Hepatocyte_AZ, Caco2_Wang); Cl.Hep. and Caco2 are reported as errors (↓).
MANTRA
NAME, ORIENT, β₁, β₂Purely topological tasks on 43,000+ manifold triangulations: homeomorphism type, orientability and Betti numbers.

Graph datasets are lifted to higher-order domains with standard cycle-based (cell) and clique-complex (simplicial) liftings.

Protocol

  • Five stratified splits per dataset with a 50/25/25 train/validation/test ratio.
  • The configuration with the best average validation score over five seeds is selected; test mean ± std is reported.
  • Metrics follow each task’s optimization direction: ↑ accuracy/F1, ↓ error.
  • Significance: best mean in bold; blue marks no statistically significant difference at the 95% level (two-sided Z-test for times).
  • Hardware: Linux, 256 logical cores, 1.5 TB RAM, 4 × NVIDIA H100 (94 GB).

CWN under TopoBench vs its original protocol · Table 12

AspectOriginal CWNTopoBench (this paper)
Data split10-fold CV (90% train)50/25/25 train/val/test
Hyperparameter searchPer-dataset, bespokeShared 5-axis grid, all models
Learning rate scheduleModel-specificFixed across models
Encoders / readoutsModel-specificShared across models

Reported CWN numbers match TopoBench’s reproducibility reports within one standard deviation. Reverting only NCI1’s split to CWN’s 10-fold cross-validation raised accuracy from 74.51 to 79.08 ± 2.50, recovering most of the gap to the originally reported 83.6; the constraints apply uniformly to HOPSE and every baseline.

Limitations

  1. Exact manual encodings such as LapPE can be expensive on massive datasets; sparse approximations or scalable neural encoders like GPSE are then preferable.
  2. Replacing topological message passing with independent MLPs yields a larger parameter footprint than baseline GNNs.
  3. The expressivity guarantees assume strict injectivity; practical instantiations with standard pooling or bounded MLPs approximate it.
  4. Spectral PSEs need symmetric operators, so Hasse graphs are made undirected and reciprocal incidences lose their direction, an effect not quantified here.
  5. The strict separation over CCWL is established analytically, as no controlled expressivity benchmark for combinatorial complexes exists yet.
